task.goal: Investigate why a pond's afternoon oxygen readings appear lower after rain.
hard_constraints: Two volunteers can sample at three accessible points over four weekends; no boat or chemical dosing.
Do not enter unsafe banks or infer a biological cause from a single reading.
Distinguish time-of-day, sensor calibration and runoff effects; specify repeat checks.
task.available_resources: Handheld meter, calibration solution and rainfall log.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Matched-time wet–dry comparison
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether the apparent decline survives matching sampling time and checking meter stability. Rainy afternoons may have lower oxygen because cloud cover reduces daytime photosynthesis, runoff changes pond conditions, or previous measurements occurred at different hours. These possibilities require repeated comparisons; oxygen alone cannot establish a biological cause.

Across four weekends, two volunteers visit all three accessible points in a fixed morning window and a fixed afternoon window, repeating the same schedule each sampling day. Use the same safe bank positions and reachable sampling depth. Both volunteers stay together: one operates the meter and the other records readings, time, recent rainfall and visible runoff. Never lean over unstable banks or sample during hazardous weather.

Before each round, follow the meter manufacturer's calibration procedure, using the supplied solution only if it is appropriate for that meter and measurement. Repeat the prescribed calibration check afterward. At each point, allow the reading to stabilize, then withdraw, reposition and repeat. Flag unstable duplicates or calibration failures rather than interpreting them environmentally. Record temperature and oxygen saturation only if the meter supports them.

The main comparison is afternoon oxygen after rain versus afternoon oxygen during dry conditions at the same point; the morning-to-afternoon change provides a separate check on daily timing. Keep rainfall amount and elapsed time since rain explicit instead of treating all wet visits as equivalent.

This needs only the stated equipment, a written record and sufficient volunteer time for two rounds per sampling day. Its main limitation is weather: four weekends may not supply repeated wet and dry conditions. Cloud effects, mixing and runoff may remain partly inseparable.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Start with one complete morning–afternoon circuit to inspect repeatability and calibration stability. Then seek at least two independent wet–dry comparisons. A timing explanation weakens if lower post-rain readings persist at matched hours with stable calibration. A runoff explanation weakens if the decline is pond-wide without a runoff-linked spatial pattern, although widespread runoff remains possible. If rain does not occur, report the missing comparison rather than a causal conclusion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Runoff-gradient and recovery comparison
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use differences among the three shoreline points to test whether rain introduces a localized oxygen change. Runoff can carry low-oxygen water or oxygen-demanding material, while rain can also mix pond water. A decline strongest beside visible inflow, followed by recovery, would support a runoff-associated effect without proving its chemical or biological pathway.

From safe public access, select one point near an existing visible runoff entry, one farther along the bank and one comparatively sheltered reference point. Do not enter drains, moving runoff or unsafe banks. If the accessible points do not represent different runoff exposure, this design cannot provide a strong spatial test.

Over four weekends, schedule an afternoon circuit at a consistent clock time on each available sampling day. Where rain occurs safely within that schedule, sample the first feasible afternoon afterward and repeat the following afternoon at the same time. Use dry weekends to establish whether the three points already differ without rain. Include a morning circuit on each weekend's first sampling day to check whether ordinary daily changes differ among points.

Two volunteers remain together and use the same reachable depth and stabilization procedure everywhere. Take two separately positioned readings per point. Alternate circuit direction between visits and record actual times to reveal bias from changing oxygen during the circuit. Perform manufacturer-prescribed calibration checks before and after each circuit; the available solution must be suitable for the instrument. Flag failed checks and unstable repeats.

The discriminating result is a rain-linked change in the inflow-to-reference difference beyond its dry-weather variation, particularly if that difference diminishes on a later visit. This requires no boat, dosing or additional sensors. Rain timing, unknown water movement and an imperfect reference point limit attribution.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First inspect a dry afternoon circuit and repeat it in reverse order to check whether point differences survive elapsed-time and order effects. Compare the next safe post-rain circuit with that baseline, then repeat at the same hour the following day. Seek the same pattern after a second independent rain event. If all points change similarly, or the apparent gradient reverses with visit order or disappears after a valid calibration check, localized runoff is not supported by these observations.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Separate oxygen solubility from oxygen depletion
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether the apparent afternoon decline reflects temperature-dependent oxygen solubility rather than a comparable decline in oxygen saturation. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen at equilibrium. Rain can change temperature through runoff and mixing, but its direction must be measured: cooler post-rain water would predict higher equilibrium oxygen concentration, so cooling alone cannot explain a lower concentration.

This alternative requires the handheld meter to display water temperature and either oxygen saturation or dissolved oxygen concentration that can be converted using the manufacturer's guidance. Inspect its capabilities first. Without temperature measurement, the supplied resources cannot resolve this mechanism; report that limitation rather than assuming a temperature change. Saturation calculations must use appropriate pressure and salinity settings; unknown or changing salinity limits interpretation.

Across four weekends, the two volunteers stay together and sample all three accessible points during fixed morning and afternoon windows on both days when feasible. Use stable bank positions and the same safely reachable depth; skip hazardous weather or unsafe access. Record actual time, rainfall amount and time since rain, temperature, oxygen concentration, saturation if available, and visible runoff. Alternate circuit direction between days to expose sampling-order effects.

Before and after each circuit, perform the manufacturer's prescribed calibration or verification procedure. Use the available calibration solution only if appropriate for this oxygen meter. At each point, let readings stabilize, then withdraw and reposition the probe for a second reading. Flag calibration failures and inconsistent duplicates.

Compare wet and dry afternoons at each point, then compare morning-to-afternoon changes. Examine whether any remaining saturation decline is concentrated near visible runoff. This distinguishes a thermal explanation from timing, instrument instability and runoff association, although it cannot identify a biological pathway.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Begin with one morning–afternoon circuit to verify that temperature and oxygen readings are repeatable. For subsequent matched-hour wet–dry comparisons, inspect concentration alongside saturation: a concentration decline with approximately unchanged saturation is consistent with solubility effects; a repeatable saturation decline challenges that explanation. Seek repetition across at least two independent rain events and dry visits. A decline despite cooler water also falsifies cooling alone as the explanation. If four weekends lack suitable rain or valid calibration checks, leave the result unresolved.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check whether rain redistributes oxygen between reachable depths
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether lower afternoon readings reflect a change in which water layer reaches the probe. Rain and wind can mix oxygen-poor deeper water upward, or runoff can form a shallow layer with different oxygen levels. A fixed shoreline reading can therefore fall without showing whether oxygen declined throughout the pond. This mechanism predicts changes in the difference between depths; it does not establish why deeper water has low oxygen.

First inspect whether the meter's probe and cable permit sampling at two repeatable, safely reachable depths from each of the three accessible points. Use a shallow submerged position and a deeper position directly beneath it, keeping both clear of sediment. Never wade, lean beyond stable footing or improvise an unsafe extension. If only one depth is reachable, this alternative cannot discriminate vertical redistribution.

Across four weekends, sample on both days in fixed morning and afternoon windows. The two volunteers stay together: one handles the probe while the other records actual times, depths, rainfall amount and elapsed time since rain, visible runoff and obvious cloud or wind changes. Alternate which depth is measured first. Allow stabilization and repeat each depth after repositioning. Follow manufacturer-prescribed calibration checks before and after each circuit, using the supplied solution only if suitable; flag failed checks.

Compare matched-hour wet and dry observations at each point. A smaller depth difference after rain, with shallow oxygen falling while deeper oxygen rises, supports redistribution within the sampled layer. A shallow change concentrated near visible runoff instead supports a runoff-associated surface effect. Morning–afternoon comparisons check timing separately.

The plan needs only the existing meter, adequate cable reach and written records. Accessible shoreline depths may miss the relevant layers, and these readings cannot estimate the pond's total oxygen inventory.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Begin with one dry afternoon circuit to establish whether depth differences exceed variation between repeated readings. Seek matched-hour checks after two independent rain events, including a repeat the following day where weekend timing allows. Use the shallow-only result as the comparator: does adding depth reveal a reproducible convergence or reversal hidden by that reading? Uniform declines at both depths weaken redistribution within the sampled layer. Unstable repeats, failed calibration checks or insufficient wet–dry observations leave the explanation unresolved.

EXPAND.title: Test whether probe response creates the apparent decline
EXPAND.proposal:
Rain may change suspended debris or local water movement, affecting probe fouling, equilibration or flow requirements. A correctly calibrated meter can still give biased field readings if its measurement procedure is unsuitable. This route tests that measurement link before interpreting the pond biologically.

Before starting, check the meter instructions for immersion, stabilization, cleaning and any required probe movement. Use calibration solution only if specified for this instrument. Over four weekends, both volunteers visit the same three safe bank positions in fixed morning and afternoon windows on available sampling days. One operates the meter; the other records actual time, rainfall amount and elapsed time since rain, visible runoff, probe condition and readings. Maintain the same reachable depth. Stay together and cancel visits during hazardous weather or where footing is unsafe.

At each point, first reproduce the previous measurement procedure if it is safe and permitted by the manufacturer. Then withdraw and reinsert the probe, following the prescribed stabilization and movement procedure, and repeat independently. Alternate procedure order between visits. Never deliberately stir sediment or aerate the sample. If visible fouling occurs, clean only as instructed and repeat the check. Perform manufacturer-prescribed calibration checks before and after each round; failed checks invalidate environmental comparisons.

Compare the procedure difference across repeated wet and dry visits at matched hours. Continue examining runoff-associated differences among points after accounting for procedure effects. This requires the stated meter, appropriate calibration solution, its instructions and written records. It can identify measurement artifacts but cannot establish a biological pathway. If historical technique cannot be reconstructed, conclusions apply only to the tested procedures.
EXPAND.experiment: On the first weekend, the meter operator runs paired procedures at all three points while the recorder tracks extra time and repeatability. Compare with the simpler matched-time, calibrated sampling route. Stop the added procedure comparison if both procedures already coincide, or if it requires unapproved handling; retain the prescribed method. Repeat any apparent wet-specific discrepancy on another wet visit and a dry visit. If the discrepancy is absent or too small to explain the observed decline, this route adds work without explaining the pattern. If rain is unavailable, report that the rain-specific artifact remains untested.

EXPAND.title: Test whether rain redistributes oxygen vertically near shore
EXPAND.proposal:
Rain-driven mixing or incoming water could change which water layer the probe samples. Afternoon oxygen might fall at the usual shallow depth while deeper reachable water changes differently. A repeatable change in the vertical profile would reveal redistribution that a single-depth wet–dry comparison could miss; it would not prove whole-pond oxygen loss or a biological cause.

First inspect the three accessible points from firm ground. Proceed only if the existing meter can safely measure at two reproducible submerged depths without extra equipment, leaning out, entering water or touching sediment. Choose a shallow and a deeper reachable position at each point and record their depths below the current surface. Record visible changes in water level against an existing bank feature. If safe depth separation is impossible, this alternative is unsuitable.

Across four weekends, sample in fixed morning and afternoon windows on available sampling days. Two volunteers remain together: one handles the meter, while the other records actual time, depth, oxygen, rainfall amount, elapsed time since rain and visible runoff. At each point, measure shallow, deeper, then shallow again, allowing manufacturer-prescribed stabilization. Reverse the sequence on the next visit. Repeat suspect readings after repositioning. Avoid disturbing the bottom and stop immediately if access deteriorates.

Check calibration before and after each circuit using the manufacturer's method and suitable solution. Flag failed checks rather than interpreting profiles. Compare wet and dry profiles separately at matched hours and examine whether changes are strongest near visible runoff. Temperature readings can help if the meter supplies them, but are not required.

The prerequisites are adequate probe reach and repeated wet and dry conditions. Shallow shoreline profiles may poorly represent the pond interior; uniform profile declines leave oxygen loss, transport and other explanations unresolved.
EXPAND.experiment: During the first safe circuit, the operator measures both depths while the recorder compares added time, stability and reach with ordinary single-depth sampling. Stop depth profiling wherever separation is negligible, sediment is disturbed or handling becomes awkward. Continue only where safe profiles are reproducible. Seek a repeated post-rain change in the shallow–deep difference, supported by return readings and absent calibration drift. If both depths track together, or differences disappear when depth order reverses, profiling provides no explanatory improvement over matched-time single-depth sampling. Require another independent rain event before treating redistribution as supported; otherwise report the result as preliminary.

EXPAND.title: Matched-time comparisons with a usable weather contrast
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of the matched-time wet–dry route: retain morning and afternoon sampling, but require a comparable dry visit before interpreting a wet–dry difference. Matching the hour alone can mistake a gradual change across four weekends for a rain effect.

Across four weekends, the two volunteers sample all three accessible points in fixed morning and afternoon windows on available weekend days. They stay together on firm banks, use the same reachable depth, record actual times, and take two independently repositioned, stabilized readings at each point. The operator follows the meter's calibration instructions before and checks it after each circuit, using the supplied solution only if suitable. The recorder logs rainfall amount, time since rain, visible runoff and cloud conditions. Stop for hazardous weather or unsafe access; flag failed calibration checks and unstable repeats.

The changed action belongs to the recorder: match each post-rain visit to the nearest dry visit at the same points and sampling window, checking whether their recent rainfall histories actually differ. Use dry observations on both sides when available to inspect background change. Treat the rain event, rather than each shoreline point, as the independent repeat. Compare morning-to-afternoon changes separately from matched-hour wet–dry changes; examine whether departures concentrate near visible runoff.

If a dry visit follows rain closely enough that runoff or recovery is still evident, label its status uncertain rather than using it as the dry control. If suitable comparisons are missing, retain the observations but withhold a rain attribution. This adds record review rather than extra trips. It reduces misleading comparisons but may leave fewer usable observations. Cloud cover, runoff and mixing can still overlap, and oxygen readings alone cannot establish a biological cause.
EXPAND.experiment: On the first weekend, the operator checks whether duplicate readings and calibration checks are repeatable while the recorder verifies that both daily windows are practical. Stop interpreting environmental differences if the prescribed checks fail; correct the meter procedure and repeat before resuming comparisons. Over the remaining weekends, seek two independent rain events with usable matched-hour dry comparisons. Inspect whether the apparent decline survives those comparisons and exceeds ordinary duplicate variation. If weather supplies only one event or no suitable dry control, report a preliminary pattern or an unresolved comparison, respectively. Relative to the source, the trial tests whether stricter comparison eligibility prevents a conclusion driven by background change without requiring more visits.

EXPAND.title: Bracket runoff gradients with a repeated reference reading
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of the runoff-gradient route: measure the reference point at both the beginning and end of each circuit. Alternating circuit direction between visits does not establish whether oxygen changed during a particular circuit; such drift can imitate a spatial runoff gradient.

Use three safe accessible bank points: an apparent runoff entry, a farther point and a comparatively sheltered reference. The prerequisite is a meaningful difference in runoff exposure visible from safe ground. If the accessible points lack that contrast, use them for pond-wide matched-time observations and do not claim a localized runoff test.

Across four weekends, sample in fixed afternoon windows on available weekend days, including the first safe scheduled afternoon after rain and the following afternoon when available. Include a morning circuit on each weekend's first sampling day to inspect time-of-day changes. Both volunteers remain together; one operates the meter and the other records actual times, rainfall amount, elapsed time since rain and visible runoff. Use fixed reachable depths, stabilized independently repositioned duplicates, and manufacturer-prescribed calibration checks before and after circuits. Use calibration solution only if appropriate. Never enter runoff, water or unstable banks.

The changed procedure is reference–two other points–reference, alternating the order of the middle points between visits. The recorder compares the reference's start-to-end change with the apparent spatial difference and duplicate variation. If reference drift could account for the gradient, mark that circuit inconclusive for spatial attribution and repeat the bracketed circuit at the next scheduled window. Do not assume a linear correction. If the reference itself receives runoff, withdraw its control status.

A repeated rain-associated increase in the inflow-to-reference difference, followed by recovery, supports localized runoff association without identifying its biological or chemical pathway. Compared with the source, one extra stop per circuit costs time but directly checks a confound that between-visit order reversal can miss.
EXPAND.experiment: On the first dry afternoon, the operator completes one bracketed circuit while the recorder assesses extra time, duplicate stability and reference drift. Abandon the added stop if it compromises safe access or completion within the sampling window; retain ordinary matched-time observations and mark spatial attribution limited. Apply the same procedure after rain and at the next scheduled afternoon. Seek a consistent gradient beyond dry-weather spatial variation on a second independent rain event. Stop interpreting a circuit's gradient whenever calibration fails, the reference loses its control status, or its drift could explain the difference. Uniform declines remain compatible with widespread runoff and other pond-wide causes.

EXPAND.title: Check whether temperature changes oxygen capacity
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: test temperature-dependent oxygen solubility. Several prior routes implicitly treat a lower oxygen concentration as evidence of a changed oxygen balance after measurement and timing checks. That assumption can fail: warmer water holds less oxygen at the same percentage saturation. Temperature therefore offers a distinct physical explanation, although rain-induced cooling would predict the opposite direction.

This route requires the existing handheld meter to provide reliable dissolved oxygen concentration, water temperature and percentage saturation with its required compensation settings. The operator first checks the instrument instructions. If those outputs or settings are unavailable, do not estimate missing quantities from unsupported assumptions; use matched-time concentration sampling and report the solubility explanation as untested. No additional instrument or chemical dosing is needed.

Across four weekends, both volunteers visit all three accessible points in fixed morning and afternoon windows on available weekend days. Remain together on firm banks and use the same safe reachable depth. The operator takes two independently repositioned readings after temperature and oxygen stabilize, following prescribed calibration and pre/post checks with suitable calibration material. The recorder logs all supported outputs, actual times, rainfall amount, time since rain, cloud conditions and visible runoff. Cancel unsafe visits and exclude failed checks from environmental comparisons.

Compare wet and dry afternoons at each point and inspect morning-to-afternoon changes separately. Lower concentration accompanied by higher temperature and similar saturation is compatible with a solubility contribution. Lower concentration despite cooling, especially with lower saturation, cannot be explained by reduced temperature-dependent capacity alone. Examine whether the pattern is localized near runoff or shared across points.

Compared with concentration-only sampling, this adds little field work if the meter already supplies these outputs. Saturation is calculated from the same sensor system, so it is not independent confirmation; compensation errors and simultaneous mixing or oxygen consumption remain possible. No biological cause follows from one reading.
EXPAND.experiment: During the first circuit, the operator verifies available outputs and manufacturer-required compensation, while the recorder checks whether duplicate temperature, concentration and saturation readings stabilize together. Stop this route if the meter cannot support the comparison reliably; continue the simpler matched-time plan. Seek the same concentration–temperature–saturation relationship on repeated wet and dry visits, preferably across two independent rain events. A lower concentration with warmer water and stable saturation supports a capacity contribution; a decline with cooler water rejects that explanation as sufficient. If differences are within instrument uncertainty or duplicate variation, classify the result as unresolved rather than assigning a mechanism.
